problems.title: Ammonia
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (24 points, 7.5% of the total). Ammonia

The Haber–Bosch process to produce ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is one of the most impactful industrial processes in history and estimated to sustain around half of today’s population. The process typically occurs at constant temperature and pressure, $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{bar}$, respectively. Equilibrium between the reactants and the product is established over Fe-based catalysts in the reactor.

The standard gas phase thermochemistry data of $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{H2}$, and $\ce{NH3}$ are shown below. Assume the enthalpy and entropy of the reaction are temperature independent.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} & \ce{N2(g)} & \ce{H2(g)} & \ce{NH3(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ/(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 0 & 0 & -45.9 \\ \hline S^\circ/(\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & 191.6 & 130.7 & 192.8 \end{array}$$

1.1 (7 pt) Find the molar nitrogen conversion (in percent) to ammonia under the production conditions from a stoichiometric mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen. Show your calculations for partial credit. If you cannot find a result, use 66% in subsequent calculations.

One of the reactants in the Haber–Bosch process is hydrogen, mainly produced by steam reforming of methane. The two-step process starts with $\ce{CH4}$ reacting with water to produce $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{CO}$. In a subsequent step, $\ce{CO}$ reacts with water to form $\ce{CO2}$ and additional hydrogen.

1.2 (2 pt) Write the overall reaction equation for the combined process. Give the mass of $\ce{CO2}$ produced in the reaction per $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of $\ce{H2}$ ($m_{\ce{CO2}}$).

In reality, $7.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of carbon dioxide is produced for each $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of hydrogen in steam reforming. The generated ammonia is classified based on $\ce{CO2}$ management. For "gray" ammonia, the $\ce{CO2}$ is released in the atmosphere; for "blue" ammonia, it is captured and stored. "Green" ammonia is made from hydrogen produced without carbon emissions.

1.3 (3 pt) Calculate the mass of the carbon dioxide ($m_{\ce{CO2},\,\text{blue}}$) that needs to be captured to produce 40,000 kg of “blue” ammonia. Assume that carbon dioxide only comes from a real steam reforming process. Assume further that the ammonia is produced at equilibrium from a stoichiometric mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen.

Using cheap renewable hydrogen, the prospect of converting it with captured $\ce{CO2}$ into methanol appears promising. However, in this procedure, there is a competing reaction that produces $\ce{CO}$:

$$\ce{CO2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g) + H2O(g)}$$

$$\ce{CO2(g) + H2(g) <=> CO(g) + H2O(g)}$$

Into a reactor maintained at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $50\,\mathrm{bar}$, a mixture containing $\ce{CO2}:\ce{H2}$ in a molar ratio of $1:4$ is fed. It has been found that the $\ce{CO2}$ conversion is 30% and the $\ce{H2}$ conversion is 18.5% when these two reactions are at equilibrium. No other processes need to be considered.

1.4 (5 pt) Calculate the thermodynamic equilibrium constants (at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) of the two reactions.

Heterogeneous copper-containing catalysts are commonly used for $\ce{CO2}$ hydrogenation. Two specific, Cu-containing catalysts ($A$ and $B$) showed promise for converting $\ce{CO2}$ to methanol. These catalysts differ not only in their catalytic rates, but also in surface area, Cu content, and Cu dispersion (the ratio of surface Cu to the total Cu in the catalyst).

Cu dispersion is important, because only Cu species at the surface are active in $\ce{CO2}$ hydrogenation. Under this assumption, 1 mole of active sites corresponds to 1 mole of surface Cu. The efficiency of these active sites is shown by their turnover frequencies ($TOF$, moles of product formed per moles of active site in a given time).

The table below reports the performance (reported as mass of produced methanol per total catalyst mass in a given time) and the specific surface areas of the two catalysts. The Cu content and dispersion of the catalysts was also measured and reported as follows:

1. At the start, all the copper in the catalysts (oxidized beforehand) is present as Cu(II); that was fully reduced to Cu(0) with hydrogen. No other species in the catalysts reacted with hydrogen besides copper oxides.
2. $\ce{N2O}$ was introduced to the reduced samples at room temperature. At this temperature, $\ce{N2O}$ only oxidizes active surface sites to Cu(I).
3. The Cu(I) active surface sites were reduced again to Cu(0) with hydrogen.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-1-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Catalyst performance} \\ (\mathrm{g_{MeOH}\,g_{cat}^{-1}\,h^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Specific surface area} \\ (\mathrm{m^2\,g_{cat}^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\ce{H2}\text{ consumed in} \\ \text{step 1 }(\mathrm{mmol\,g_{cat}^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\ce{H2}\text{ consumed in} \\ \text{step 3 }(\mathrm{mmol\,g_{cat}^{-1}})\end{array} \\ \hline \text{Catalyst } A & 0.80 & 100 & 5.0 & 0.30 \\ \hline \text{Catalyst } B & 0.90 & 120 & 4.0 & 0.70 \end{array}$$

1.5 (3 pt) Find the methanol production rate per total mass of Cu (in $\mathrm{g_{MeOH}\,g_{Cu}^{-1}\,h^{-1}}$) for catalysts $A$ and $B$.

1.6 (3 pt) Find the $TOF$ (in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$) for catalysts $A$ and $B$. If you cannot find results, use $TOF_\text{Catalyst A} = 100\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ and $TOF_\text{Catalyst B} = 1\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ in subsequent calculations.

1.7 (1 pt) Indicate the correct statement on the answer sheet.
a. Catalyst $A$ has more efficient active sites.
b. Catalyst $B$ has more efficient active sites.
c. The two catalysts have active sites with the same efficiency.

problems.title: Electronic nose
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (12 points, 6% of the total). Electronic nose

Resistive gas sensors, especially those using semiconducting metal oxides (SMOX), are becoming increasingly popular. They can detect tiny amounts of impurities, are small and stable, and are easy to make and use. These features make SMOX sensors stand out among the many types of gas sensors that work on different physical and chemical principles.

The mixed oxide $\mathbf{X}$ that has the normal spinel crystal structure, $\mathrm{A^{2+}B^{3+}{}_2O^{2-}{}_4}$, is an example of one of these SMOX materials. $\mathbf{X}$ can be obtained by decomposition of the crystalline hydrated metal oxalate $\mathbf{Z}\ce{C2O4}\cdot k\ce{H2O}$ of metal $\mathbf{Z}$ on air. When heated to $140\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the crystalline hydrate loses 19.7% of its mass. Further heating in air leads to the formation of $2.407\,\mathrm{g}$ of black colored $\mathbf{X}$ at $500\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $3.8\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of carbon dioxide at $101325\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

2.1 (4 pt) Determine the formula of $\mathbf{X}$ and the value of $\boldsymbol{k}$ in $\mathbf{Z}\ce{C2O4}\cdot k\ce{H2O}$.

In the spinel structures oxygen atoms form a face centered cubic (FCC) lattice. In normal spinels the $\mathrm{A^{2+}}$ cations occupy part of the tetrahedral, and the $\mathrm{B^{3+}}$ cations occupy part of the octahedral lattice sites.

2.2 (2 pt) Calculate the percentage of the tetrahedral sites that is occupied in the case of a normal spinel $\mathrm{A^{2+}B^{3+}{}_2O^{2-}{}_4}$.

In addition to the normal spinels, the $\mathrm{MM'_2O_4}$ general formula also describes the inverse and the mixed spinel structures. Here M are the tetrahedrally coordinated, M′ the octahedrally coordinated cations, but contrary to normal spinels, particular cations are not restricted to a single lattice site. A characteristic of the inverse spinel structures is that the electron configuration of the M′ site cations is $\mathrm{d^0}$, $\mathrm{d^5}$ or $\mathrm{d^{10}}$.

2.3 (1 pt) Select on the answer sheet two of the given formulas, which correspond to the structure of inverse spinel: $\ce{Fe3O4}$, $\ce{NiFe2O4}$, $\ce{Mn3O4}$, $\ce{FeCr2O4}$.

Semiconductors are materials whose orbitals contain a small excess or deficit of electrons, leading to negative or positive charges (holes), respectively. These charges can move through the semiconductor and allow it to conduct electricity. Chemical reactions can increase or decrease the charge on a semiconductor, altering its conductivity.

$\mathbf{X}$ is an example of a semiconductor where electricity is carried by positive charges (holes). For a resistive gas sensor based on $\mathbf{X}$, the resistance $R$ is measured over time $t$, while passing a gas over the sensor. This allows redox reactions to occur between the gas and the semiconductor surface, which will change the resistance of the sensor depending on the donor/acceptor properties of the gas. Figure 1 shows the two different types of signal obtained this way.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-2-fig1.png

Figure 1: plot of resistance against time for two possible signal types, (a) and (b). Grey bars = air, white bars = air + analyte gas.

2.4 (2 pt) Correlate the signal type (a or b) obtained from the $\mathbf{X}$ based sensor with the analyte gases ($\ce{H2S}$, $\ce{O3}$, $\ce{NO2}$, $\ce{NH3}$) during their detection at low concentrations.

The dependence of the specific conductivity ($\sigma$) of $\mathbf{X}$ on temperature is described by the Arrhenius law: $\sigma(T) = \sigma_0 \exp(-E_a/(RT))$, where $E_a$ is the activation energy of conductivity. Three types of conductivity can be distinguished in different temperature ranges:

Ionization (I): 444–570 K, Impurity (II): 585–765 K, and Intrinsic (III): 800–905 K.

The sketch below illustrates the conductivity-temperature relation for the three temperature ranges.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-2-fig2.png

2.5 (3 pt) Based on the sketch above, order the activation energies associated with the different conductivity types, $E_a(I)$, $E_a(II)$, and $E_a(III)$, from largest to smallest.

problems.title: Tyrosinase
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (31 points, 7.5% of the total). Tyrosinase

The enzyme tyrosine 3-monooxygenase has an important biological role because it catalyzes the initial and rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of the neurotransmitter dopamine. In this first step, L-DOPA is produced from the amino acid L-tyrosine (Tyr) in the presence of dissolved oxygen, tetrahydrofolic acid and ferrous ions. In a subsequent step, another enzyme transforms L-DOPA into dopamine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-3-fig1.png

The activity of the tyrosine 3-monooxygenase enzyme is described well by the simplest model of enzyme action, the Michaelis-Menten equation. This gives the rate of the formation ($r$) of L-DOPA as a function of the enzyme (E) and substrate Tyr (S) concentrations as follows:

$$r = \frac{k[\mathrm{E}][\mathrm{S}]}{K_\mathrm{M} + [\mathrm{S}]}$$

The following values of enzymatic turnover frequency ($k = 250\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$) and Michaelis constant ($K_\mathrm{M} = 0.49\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$) can be used in this task when needed.

Catechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene) inactivates the enzyme tyrosine 3-monooxygenase irreversibly by turning it into an inactive form. When a carefully purified sample of catechol is mixed with the enzyme with the exclusion of dissolved oxygen, no change is seen at all. So the reaction of catechol with dissolved oxygen, which produces o-quinone, must be important.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-3-fig2.png

This process can be studied in the absence of the enzyme. A test experiment in a reactor not in contact with ambient air at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at pH 7.5 gave the following kinetic data:

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{time} \\ (\mathrm{min})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{catechol concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{oxygen concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}o\text{-quinone concentration} \\ (\mathrm{\mu mol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} \\ \hline 0 & 2.00 & 0.200 & 0 \\ \hline 20.0 & 1.97 & 0.170 & 30 \\ \hline 40.0 & 1.94 & 0.140 & 60 \\ \hline 60.0 & 1.91 & 0.111 & 89 \\ \hline 80.0 & 1.88 & 0.083 & 117 \\ \hline 100.0 & 1.85 & 0.054 & 146 \end{array}$$

3.1 (5.0 pt) Identify the only by-product (which is not one of the molecules shown in the table above) and write the balanced equation of the process with molecular formulas based on the kinetic data.

3.2 (2.0 pt) Calculate the initial rate ($r_0$) of o-quinone formation in this experiment with an appropriate unit.

The rate law of the process was determined by varying the initial concentrations of the reactants. Changing the oxygen concentration did not influence the initial rate of the process. Using different catechol concentrations gave the following initial rates for o-quinone formation:

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{catechol concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{initial rate of } o\text{-quinone formation} \\ (\mathrm{\mu mol\,dm^{-3}\,min^{-1}})\end{array} \\ \hline 1.0 & 0.75 \\ \hline 4.0 & 3.0 \\ \hline 6.0 & 4.5 \\ \hline 8.0 & 6.0 \\ \hline 10.0 & 7.5 \end{array}$$

3.3 (5.0 pt) Determine the rate law of the reaction between catechol and oxygen producing o-quinone. Calculate the rate constant of this process ($k_\text{catechol}$) with an appropriate unit.

In separate experiments, it was confirmed that neither o-quinone, nor the by-product inactivates the enzyme alone, nor even in combination.

An experiment in which the enzyme is reacted with catechol in the presence of dissolved oxygen did show inactivation, though.

The experiment was done in an open vessel so that any oxygen consumed in the process could be continuously replenished from air. The initial concentration of the enzyme was $4.2\,\mathrm{nmol\,dm^{-3}}$, the initial concentration of catechol was $2.00\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$ at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at pH 7.5.

Samples were taken regularly from the enzyme-catechol reaction mixture, and the activity of the enzyme was assayed by adding L-tyrosine, tetrahydrofolic acid and ferrous ion. During the enzyme activity measurements, the concentration of added L-tyrosine was $10.0\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$ and the concentration of L-DOPA in each assay sample was measured after 2.0 minutes. The following results were obtained:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-3-fig3.png

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{inactivation reaction time} \\ t\ (\mathrm{min})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{L-DOPA concentration after 2.0 minutes from the start of the assay} \\ {[\text{DOPA}]}\ (\mathrm{\mu mol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} \\ \hline 0 & 2.0 \\ \hline 20.0 & 1.9 \\ \hline 40.0 & 1.7 \\ \hline 60.0 & 1.3 \\ \hline 70.0 & 1.00 \\ \hline 80.0 & 0.72 \\ \hline 90.0 & 0.38 \end{array}$$

3.4 (4.0 pt) Derive a formula that allows you to calculate the actual concentration of active enzyme ([E]) from the data of these experiments in terms of $k$ ($= 250\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$), $K_\mathrm{M}$ ($= 0.49\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$), and/or reagent concentrations.

The change in the active enzyme concentration as a function of time is well described by a parabola ($[\mathrm{E}] = [\mathrm{E}]_0 - k_\text{obs} t^2$), where $k_\text{obs}$ is an observed rate constant (i.e. one that can be written later as a combination of elementary rate constants and initial concentrations), and $[\mathrm{E}]_0$ is the initial concentration of the enzyme.

3.5 (3.0 pt) Give the value of $k_\text{obs}$ with an appropriate unit.

3.6 (3.0 pt) Determine the first half-life of the enzyme inactivation reaction. Derive a formula that gives the first half-life as a function of the initial enzyme concentration and of $k_\text{obs}$.

The first half-lives for enzyme inactivation were determined using other initial catechol concentrations. The dependences of active enzyme concentrations on time were very well described by parabolas in these cases as well.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{catechol concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{first half-life} \\ (\mathrm{min})\end{array} \\ \hline 1.0 & 140 \\ \hline 4.0 & 35 \\ \hline 6.0 & 23 \\ \hline 8.0 & 17.5 \\ \hline 10.0 & 14 \end{array}$$

3.7 (6.0 pt) Derive a rate equation of the enzyme inactivation process consistent with all the experimental observations.

3.8 (3.0 pt) What are the reactants of the rate determining step for the enzyme inactivation process? Select the ONLY correct option on the answer sheet.
A) catechol + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
B) catechol + o-quinone → ...
C) o-quinone + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
D) enzyme + 2 catechol → ...
E) enzyme + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
F) 2 catechol + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
G) enzyme + catechol → ...
H) enzyme + by-product → ...

problems.title: Potassium
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (21 points, 6% of the total). Potassium

Elementary potassium was the first metal synthesized by electrolysis (1807). Humphry Davy used voltaic cells and electrodes immersed into molten $\ce{KOH}$.

4.1 (2 pt) Give balanced equations for the processes taking place on the cathode (1) and the anode (2).

It is little known that only a year after Davy, French chemists have produced potassium in a chemical reduction. One of the methods involved a mixture of potassium carbonate and finely powdered carbon. This mixture was heated to very high temperatures in a gun barrel. Carbon monoxide and potassium vapors were leaving the end of the barrel, where the metal could be condensed to a solid.

4.2 (1 pt) Write down the balanced equation for the reaction giving only these two products.

The chemical production of potassium had a low yield. Depending on the circumstances, a considerable amount of reddish paste was left behind in the gun barrel. Gmelin isolated an interesting compound ($\mathbf{X}$) from this residue in 1825 by recrystallization in water. The exact structure of the byproduct $\mathbf{X}$ was determined more than one and a half century later.

$\mathbf{X}$ is a hydrated salt (2 mol water : 1 mol of salt) forming golden yellow crystals. Its anion has an exceptionally symmetric (shown by vibrational spectra) and stable planar cyclic structure.

The diprotic acid ($\mathbf{Y}$) that can be formed from the salt $\mathbf{X}$ has surprisingly (at least to the superficial observer) low $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values: 0.8 and 2.2.

4.3 (3 pt) Give the pH where 95% of all dissolved acid $\mathbf{Y}$ is in the neutral acid form.

4.4 (4 pt) Calculate the pH of a $0.01\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ solution of the salt $\mathbf{X}$ in pure water.

The key step in the structure identification of $\mathbf{X}$ was the treatment of the anhydrous salt with methyl iodide. The salt reacted with two equivalents of methyl iodide. The somewhat volatile compound that was obtained had a molar mass of $170.12\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ (measured in a mass spectrometer).

A number of analogous salts were also identified in the mixture in smaller quantities. The appropriate potassium salts when treated with two equivalent of MeI gave derivatives with molar masses of: $142.11\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, $114.10\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, $198.13\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

4.5 (4 pt) Give the empirical formula of Gmelin’s compound $\mathbf{X}$.

4.6 (3 pt) Draw the structure of the free acid $\mathbf{Y}$.

The extraordinary stability of the series of anions in the salts analogous to X can be attributed to electron delocalization.

4.7 (4 pt) Draw one resonance structure with a significant contribution for the anion in each of the four salts.

problems.title: Unknown
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (44 points, 6% of the total). Unknown

Metal containing salt $\mathbf{A}$ can be prepared in a simple exchange reaction when the cold, saturated aqueous solutions of the two distinctly colored compounds, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are mixed in stoichiometric ratio. $10.00\,\mathrm{g}$ $\mathbf{B}$ in solution mixed with the solution of $12.86\,\mathrm{g}$ $\mathbf{C}$, and immediately cooled to $2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ will give $4.90\,\mathrm{g}$ solid $\mathbf{A}$. The yield of $\mathbf{A}$ is 32.6 %.

To determine the composition of $\mathbf{A}$, first iodometry is performed. A known mass of $\mathbf{A}$ is added to a titration flask, acidified with sulfuric acid, then KI is added in excess and there is a precipitate formation. After a few minutes, sodium citrate solution is added until the solution is free of precipitate. The citrate ions form a strong complex with a metal ion present in the mixture, reversing completely the reaction leading to the precipitate. The resulting mixture is titrated with sodium thiosulfate solution (Titration I via reaction 1). To the blue titrated solution another portion of sulfuric acid (significantly more than the initial amount) is added to protonate the citrate. The previous solid precipitate is formed once again [reaction 2]. The mixture is titrated with the same thiosulfate solution (titration II via reaction 1).

The average volumes for $100.0\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\mathbf{A}$ with $5.000\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ thiosulfate are $54.12\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in Titration I and $5.41\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in Titration II.

When the aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}$ is heated, the blue precipitate $\mathbf{D}$ can be observed [reaction 3]. Compound $\mathbf{E}$ can be crystallized from the liquid above $\mathbf{D}$. The low temperature during the synthesis of $\mathbf{A}$ is important to avoid contamination by $\mathbf{E}$.

5.1 (4.0 pt) Write balanced equations for reactions [1] and [2].

The thermal decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ was studied in detail. When pure $\mathbf{A}$ is slowly heated, already at around $75\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it explodes. When the compound is dispersed in aluminium oxide and the mixture is heated, then the matrix absorbs the excess heat, and the explosion can be avoided. Two decomposition steps can be observed. In the first step (at $65\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) in addition to the 14.1 % mass decrease, a two-component solid residue forms [reaction 4]. The components of this residue can be easily separated, as $\mathbf{F}$ is well soluble in water, while $\mathbf{G}$ does not dissolve at all. The $\mathbf{F}$:$\mathbf{G}$ mass ratio is $1.00:2.97$. On further heating, $\mathbf{F}$ decomposes without a solid residue [reaction 5]. That means pure $\mathbf{G}$ is the final solid decomposition product of $\mathbf{A}$. $\mathbf{G}$ contains two other elements in addition to 27.0 wt% oxygen. One of the two components of the gas mixture forming in the first decomposition step can be easily quantitated if it is absorbed in acid solution.

Some hints

• Compound $\mathbf{A}$ decomposes without releasing oxygen.
• Compound $\mathbf{A}$ contains two different metals.
• Compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ both contain a complex ion.
• $\mathbf{C}$ is a well-known compound for any chemistry student.
• Compound $\mathbf{F}$ does not contain any metal.

5.2 (28.0 pt) Give chemical formulae of $\mathbf{A}$—$\mathbf{G}$. You don’t have to show your calculations, but if your compounds are incorrect you may gain partial marks from correct calculations.

5.3 (12.0 pt) Write balanced equations for reactions [3]—[5].

problems.title: SABIC
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (23 points, 7.5% of the total). SABIC

The Saudi Basic Industries Corporation (SABIC) was established in the mid-1970s as part of Saudi Arabia's plan to diversify its economy. Today, SABIC is a global chemical giant, producing 69 million tons of products annually.

Part A

SABIC's own unique ethene oligomerization technology (oligomers are polymers with few monomer units) produces linear alpha olefins (1-alkenes), which are used in numerous industrial applications.

Linear alpha olefins are produced by catalytic oligomerization of ethene, resulting in a range of chain lengths with a distribution. Different catalysts can yield various distributions of products.

In the geometric or Schulz–Flory distribution, each oligomer fraction is related to the previous fraction by the equation, $T_{n+1} = \alpha T_n$, where $T_n$ represents the molar amount of the oligomer with $n$ ethene units, and $\alpha$ is a constant called the probability of chain propagation. Ethene, the monomer is not a member of the series ($n \geq 2$).

One catalytic oligomerization process can be described by a relatively simple mechanism:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig1.png

Although this mechanism is not a classical chain reaction because the final product is not produced within the cycle, the usual kinetic treatment of chain reactions can be applied to it. The three processes shown (1–3) are all chain propagation steps. R is lengthened by each cycle.

All three reactions are first order with respect to the chain carriers. For ethene, use an unknown order $\rho$, to be determined later.

7.1 (1 pt) Write the rate equations for reactions 1–3 using $k_1$, $k_2$, and $k_3$ as the corresponding rate constants, which are independent of the carbon chain length.

Chain termination step, producing the oligomers, is a first order reaction competing with reaction 1.

7.2 (2 pt) Write i) the chemical equation and ii) rate equation of termination. Use $k_t$ as the corresponding rate constant.

7.3 (4 pt) Find the value of $\rho$ which ensures that the product mixture of olefins shows the required ratio of products in accordance with the Schulz–Flory distribution when the reaction is run in a closed system. Derive a formula for this case that gives $\alpha$ as the function of rate constants.

Aluminum alkyls are used as co-catalysts in the ethene oligomerization process. It was found that they also catalyzed the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of the aromatic solvents used for the oligomerization.

In a typical oligomerization reaction, an alkylated aromatic compound $\mathbf{Q}$ was isolated from the complex reaction mixture of ethene oligomerization in toluene as solvent. The alkylated aromatic compound $\mathbf{Q}$ has the molecular formula $\ce{C11H16}$ and its $^1$H NMR spectrum contains the following peaks.

$^1$H NMR of $\mathbf{Q}$: $\delta$ 0.9 ($t$, 3H); 1.35 ($m$, 2H); 1.59 ($m$, 2H); 2.34 ($s$, 3H), 2.60 ($t$, 2H); 7.18 ($d$, 2H); 7.22 ($d$, 2H).

7.4 (3 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{Q}$.

Part B

Vitrimers are adaptive polymers with "reversible" covalent bonds, allowing shape-changing and self-healing under specific conditions. This subtask explores the principles of vitrimer chemistry, an important topic in SABIC's polymer research.

A recently elucidated fast and reversible reaction involving dioxaborolanes can serve as the chemical background for such an adaptable polymer network. The two dioxaborolanes below were prepared by the reaction of phenylboronic acid with 1,2-butanediol and 3,5-dimethylphenylboronic acid with 1,2-propanediol, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig2.png

They participate in a model metathesis (exchange) reaction. The two carefully purified compounds were mixed in the absence of solvent and the mixture was kept at $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for two hours. Interestingly, the gas chromatograms of the mixture at the start and at the end of the incubation period showed only the peaks below, with equimolar quantities of the components. The peaks in this system separate in a way that correlates with molar mass: compounds with lower mass appear at earlier elution times.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig3.png

No catalyst, water, diol or acid was detectable in the mixture.

7.5 (2 pt) Draw the compounds associated with peaks I–IV in the chromatogram.

Linking functional units to a polymer chain is known as grafting, and the functional units are referred to as grafting agents. In this case, the dioxaborolane units are linked to the polymer chains by maleimide groups via a radical process, in which one maleimide group is coupling to the polymer chain at a random carbon atom. The scheme below introduces a flexible synthesis route towards the dioxaborolane maleimide grafting agent used in the vitrimers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig4.png

7.7 (1 pt) Select on the answer sheet which reagent(s) and/or condition is/are appropriate for linking the dioxaborolane maleimide units to polyethylene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig5.png

The vitrimer was prepared as follows:

• Polyethylene is grafted with dioxaborolane maleimide. Assume no side reactions between the dioxaborolane maleimide compounds.
• The reagents are removed from the macromolecules.
• Propanediol functionalized bis-dioxaborolane is added to enable crosslinking.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig6.png

• The mixture is carefully heated for metathesis (exchange) reaction to take place.

To determine the extent of grafting and crosslinking in the vitrimer, infrared (IR) spectroscopy was used at room temperature where the metathesis reaction is extremely slow. Assume a homogeneous vitrimer.

• All of the small molecules are removed from the polymer.
• The IR spectrum of a thin polymer film is measured.
• IR spectrum contains absorption peaks that correspond to specific functional groups.

Problem 9 (35 points, 7.5% of the total). Porphyrin complexes

Part A. Metals in petroleum

Saudi Arabian petroleum, primarily hydrocarbons, contains elements like vanadium in porphyrin complexes, hinting at its biological origins.

Vanadium complex $\mathbf{B}$ is presumably formed in petroleum from chlorophyll according to the following scheme:

9.1 (4.0 pt) Assign the molecular formulae a–e (given in the answer sheet) to the intermediates I–V.

9.3 (1.0 pt) Indicate the oxidation state of vanadium in $\mathbf{B}$.

Part B. Porphyrin non-metal complexes

Porphyrins are known to form chelate-type complexes not only with metals but also with some non-metals, for example, with boron and phosphorus. Octaethylporphyrin ($\ce{H2}$OEP) is often used to model natural porphyrins and to study porphyrin complexes. It has the following structure and can be represented as:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig2.png

To produce dicationic planar boron porphyrin complex $[\mathbf{X3}]^{2+}$, either $\ce{BCl3}$ or another binary compound $\mathbf{X1}$ can be used as a precursor:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig3.png

9.4 (3.0 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{X1}$, intermediate complex $\mathbf{X2}$ and the product $[\mathbf{X3}]^{2+}$.

Phosphorus forms porphyrin cationic complexes $[\mathbf{Y1}]^{n+}$, $[\mathbf{Y2}]^{n+}$, and $[\mathbf{Y3}]^{n+}$. The complex $[\mathbf{Y3}]^{n+}$ has one less plane of symmetry compared to $[\mathbf{Y1}]^{n+}$ and $[\mathbf{Y2}]^{n+}$ (ignore ethyl substituents in OEP ligand when considering symmetry). Pyridine (Py) is used here as a basic solvent, “Hal” is one of the halogens: F, Cl, or Br:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig4.png

Porphyrin sandwich-type complexes form when there are several porphyrin rings aligned relative to each other. Examples are $\mathrm{Zr(OEP)_2}$, $\mathrm{Eu_2(OEP)_3}$, $\mathrm{Bi_2(OEP)_2Cl_2}$ that have at least 3 planes of symmetry each. Note that the hole size in the OEP ligand is ca. 4.0 Å, and the average metal–N distances in these complexes are 2.4, 2.5, 2.3 Å, respectively.

9.7 (3.0 pt) Suggest the structures of $\mathrm{Zr(OEP)_2}$, $\mathrm{Eu_2(OEP)_3}$, and $\mathrm{Bi_2(OEP)_2Cl_2}$. You may use a simplified representation of the OEP ligand.

Another type of porphyrin sandwich-type complex is metal–porphyrin dimers with single or multiple metal–metal bonds. The eclipsed conformation is generally preferred for metal–porphyrin dimers with 7, 8, and 9 d-electrons. Otherwise, these complexes are more stable in a staggered conformation, where the porphyrin rings are rotated relative to each other by $45^\circ$.

problems.problem:
Problem 3 (7.5% of the total). Lanterns and the Burj Khalifa

At $829.8\,\mathrm{m}$, Dubai’s Burj Khalifa is the world's tallest structure. To simplify construction, many floors were made from similar pieces. Some artificial "molecular skyscrapers" can be made through coordination chemistry of just two pieces: metal ions and organic ligands.

In these 3D structures, every vertex contains a square planar Pd(II) ion coordinated to four pyridine ligands. Along each edge is a bent organic ligand consisting of two pyridines linked together.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig1.png

The angle between the two $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds from the same ligand controls which structure forms. Larger angles give larger structures.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig2.png

Where free rotation around a bond is possible, the ligand adopts a conformation to form a structure with the smallest possible angle.

3.1 Tick the smallest angle (approximately) between the $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds which could be achieved by ligands $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig3.png

3.2 Using “<”, rank ligands $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, and $\mathbf{F}$, from smallest angle to largest angle between the $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds that they could form.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig4.png

One series of structures can be modelled as polyhedra with tetracoordinated Pd(II) ions at the vertices. All structures have eight triangular faces ($F_3$), with various numbers of square faces ($F_4$).

The triangular and square faces can be placed onto a square grid, where the relative position of two nearest triangles is described with integer coordinates $h$ and $k$. $Q$ is then given by the equation:

$$Q = h^2 + k^2$$

Part of the grid for a structure with $h = 2$ and $k = 4$ is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig5.png

The smallest possible structure in this series is an octahedron, where $Q = 1$, and $(h, k) = (0, 1)$ or $(1, 0)$. It has six vertices, eight triangular faces, and 12 edges. Nearest triangles are a move of one face in one direction apart.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig6.png

The second smallest structure is a cuboctahedron, where $Q = 2$. Nearest triangles are a move of one face in each direction apart.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig7.png

3.3 Complete the column in the table for $Q = 2$, describing the number of vertices, $V$, number of edges $E$, the total number of faces, $F$, and the number of square faces, $F_4$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} Q & 1 & 2 \\ \hline (h, k) & (0, 1)\text{ or }(1, 0) & (1, 1) \\ \hline V & 6 & \\ \hline E & 12 & \\ \hline F & 8 & \\ \hline F_3 & 8 & 8 \\ \hline F_4 & 0 & \end{array}$$

All structures obey the following rules:

$$V - E + F = 2$$

$$V = 6Q$$

$$F - V = 2$$

3.4 Complete the table for the third smallest structure, where $Q = 4$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} Q & 4 \\ \hline (h, k) & \\ \hline V & \\ \hline E & \\ \hline F & \\ \hline F_3 & 8 \\ \hline F_4 & \end{array}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig8.png

In contrast to these large structures, the smallest structures contain two metals and four ligands and are called lanterns. They are similar in shape to the traditional lanterns seen at the Dubai light festival. Lanterns are formed by ligands such as $\mathbf{L}$, which make two parallel $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds. Ligand $\mathbf{L}$ has two planes of symmetry and can adopt a planar conformation with the angles shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig9.png

Hint:

- The transformation from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{I}$ could also be achieved by Lewis acid catalysis.

3.5 Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{J}$, $\mathbf{K}$, and ligand $\mathbf{L}$.

Unlike symmetrical ligand $\mathbf{L}$, chiral ligand $\mathbf{M}$ lacks symmetry and exists as a pair of $R$ and $S$ enantiomers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig10.png

Multiple lantern isomers can be formed from ligand $\mathbf{M}$. We can group these isomers in two ways. Firstly we categorise by the number of each type of ligand in the lantern: (i) all the same ($RRRR$ or $SSSS$), (ii) one different ($RRRS$ or $SSSR$), (iii) $cis$-$RRSS$, and (iv) $trans$-$RSRS$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig11.png

problems.title: The life of tennis balls
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (6% of the total). The life of tennis balls

This problem honours the incredible Rafael Nadal, a true tennis icon who concluded his remarkable career in 2024.

The Dubai Tennis Championships is a prestigious tournament held annually in UAE. Many of the world's top players, including Rafael Nadal, Roger Federer, Novak Djokovic, and Andy Murray have won titles there.

The composition of tennis balls has evolved over hundreds of years. To ensure a good bounce, the inside of modern tennis balls is pressurised above atmospheric pressure. However, old hollow tennis balls just contained air at atmospheric pressure.

In this problem, assume tennis balls have an inner radius of $R = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ that remains constant throughout the pressurisation process. Assume that the composition of air is 20% $\ce{O2}$ and 80% $\ce{N2}$ by volume. Consider that overpressure does not expand the ball.

4.1 Calculate the mass $m$ (in g) of air inside an old tennis ball at $T_0 = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Chemists then discovered how to pressurise a ball above atmospheric pressure using a reaction between compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, which forms gas $\mathbf{C}$ (to create additional inner pressure) plus other non-gaseous products.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-4-fig1.png

A capsule with a quantity $m_\mathrm{mix} = 0.3389\,\mathrm{g}$ of a stoichiometric mixture of two white inorganic compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ was placed inside a ball filled with air at atmospheric pressure. They reacted completely inside the ball upon heating to form gas $\mathbf{C}$ and other products (reaction 1) to produce an overall pressure inside the ball of $p = 1.600\,\mathrm{atm}$ (at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Once this ball was opened, all residue inside was collected and dissolved in water. The dropping of silver nitrate in that solution gave a white precipitate (reaction 2). This collected precipitate could be partially dissolved in a concentrated aqueous solution of $\mathbf{B}$. By increasing the pH of this mixture, the precipitate dissolved completely (reaction 3). If the same initial capsule of $\mathbf{A}$+$\mathbf{B}$ is dissolved in water and concentrated solution of silver nitrate added, $m_\mathrm{precipitate} = 0.8224\,\mathrm{g}$ of white precipitate formed which was approximately twice the mass of precipitate formed in reaction 2.

When the capsule of $\mathbf{A}$+$\mathbf{B}$ dissolved in a solution of HI the formation of gas $\mathbf{D}$ started, and the solution turned brown (reaction 4). Upon further addition of sodium thiosulfate this colour disappeared (reaction 5).

The densities of gases $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ differ by no more than 10%.

4.2 Write the chemical formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{D}$.

4.3 Write equations for reactions 1-5.

The pressure inside modern tennis balls is $p_0 = 1.80\,\mathrm{atm}$. They are sold in a pressurised can, with the same pressure in the can as in the ball to stop gas coming out during storage.

Standard balls contain air and premium balls contain pure $\ce{N2}$. Once the can is opened, depressurisation begins, and the gas diffuses out of the balls until the internal pressure reaches atmospheric pressure. Assume there is no diffusion of gas into the balls at any point. The activation energy for the depressurisation of a premium ball is $E_\mathrm{A} = 50.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

The rate of ball depressurisation (pressure/time) could be described by similar equations of those used in chemical kinetics. At $T_0 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, once the can is opened, the premium balls depressurise to $p_1 = 1.40\,\mathrm{atm}$ after $t_1 = 241\,\mathrm{h}$ and to $p_2 = 1.19\,\mathrm{atm}$ after about $t_2 = 21$ days. The initial depressurisation rate of regular balls is 10% faster than premium balls.

4.4a Demonstrate that the depressurisation process follows the first kinetic order by calculating the depressurisation rate constant $k_{\ce{N2}}$ for $\ce{N2}$ in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$.
Note: If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $k_{\ce{N2}} = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ in further calculations.

4.4b Calculate the (depressurisation) rate constant $k_{\ce{O2}}$ for $\ce{O2}$ in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$, assuming the rates for both gases are additive.

As well as today being the IChO 2025 theory paper, it is also (perhaps less importantly) the Semi-Finals day at Wimbledon. Amanda Anisimova will start a match in $t_\mathrm{match} = 12.0\,\mathrm{h}$ from now. The weather today in Wimbledon is predicted to be a constant $T_\mathrm{W} = 30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume a new set of premium balls, which were manufactured and placed in the can at $T_0 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, are opened now and quickly change to $T_\mathrm{W} = 30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

4.4c Calculate the pressure $p_\mathrm{start}$ (in atm) of the balls at the start of the match.

problems.title: Solar-powered multi-stage flash desalination
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (6.5% of the total). Solar-powered multi-stage flash desalination

Freshwater is scarce in the arid climate of the UAE. The country relies on solar-powered desalination plants to produce freshwater. A Dubai desalination plant uses a multi-stage flash (MSF) desalination process. In MSF desalination, seawater is heated by passing through a series of heat exchangers to raise its temperature, reaching its saturation temperature at a high pressure. When pressure is reduced, this superheated seawater gives off pure water vapour to become saturated again, a process known as flashing.

Assume seawater in Dubai is at $T_0 = 25.00\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and is an aqueous solution of 3.45 % mass NaCl. Assume complete ionisation of NaCl in water.

The boiling point of seawater is higher than pure water. The boiling point elevation constant, $K_\mathrm{b} = 0.5120\,\mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$.

5.1 Calculate the boiling point, $T$, (in °C) of Dubai seawater at atmospheric pressure.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use a temperature of $373.50\,\mathrm{K}$ for further calculations.

5.2 Calculate the percentage mass of NaCl, $w_\mathrm{NaCl}$, in water that has a boiling point, $T_\mathrm{b} = 378.00\,\mathrm{K}$.

5.3 The boiling point of seawater also increases as pressure increases. Calculate the boiling point, $T$, (in °C) of the initial Dubai seawater at a pressure, $p = 2.50\,\mathrm{atm}$. The latent heat of vaporisation of water, $E_\mathrm{vap} = 2260\,\mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}}$ ($40.716\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$). Assume this is the same for seawater.

In the plant, a flash chamber (of volume, $V = 100\,\mathrm{L}$) contains a mass of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater (l) at $T_1 = 90.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Another mass of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater is then overheated to $T_2 = 110.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at high pressure before being added to this chamber, where a reduction in pressure causes some water to turn into steam.

After equilibrium was established, the temperature in the chamber was $T_\mathrm{f} = 97.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume there was no loss of energy, and that the latent heat of vaporisation is independent of temperature.

The specific heat capacity of seawater, $C_\mathrm{p} = 3.85\,\mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, assumed to be independent of temperature. The density of seawater, $d = 1025\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

5.4 Calculate the amount, $n$, (in mol) of water that vapourised, assuming that the latent heat of vaporization does not depend on pressure, and that the heat capacity of water vapor in the chamber is negligble.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $0.56\,\mathrm{mol}$ for further calculations.

5.5 Assuming the initial vapour pressure before addition of the overheated water in the chamber was $p_\mathrm{i} = 0.690\,\mathrm{atm}$, calculate the final vapour pressure, $p_\mathrm{f}$, (in atm) in the chamber assuming the water vapour behaves as an ideal gas.

5.6 Calculate the thermal energy, $E$, (in kWh) required to heat a mass of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater from $T_1 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $T_2 = 110.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $0.1\,\mathrm{kWh}$ for further calculations.

5.7 A plant produces $50{,}000\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of pure water per day. The plant passes Dubai seawater through 30 flash cycles and overall can extract 85% of the water present. Calculate the mass, $m$, (in kg) of Dubai seawater needed per day.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $6.0\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{kg}$ for further calculations.

Plants make efficient use of heat exchangers to save energy. We can assume the total energy required by the plant is the same as the energy needed to heat all the seawater from $T_1 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $T_2 = 110.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

5.8 Assuming a $10\,\mathrm{m^2}$ solar panel has a power of $2.00\,\mathrm{kW}$ averaged during the 12 operational hours every day and the efficiency of using energy is 67%, calculate the number of panels, $N$, required for the plant.

Problem 6 (6% of the total). Solar energy conversion by $\ce{CO2}$ reduction

Use the following data to solve this problem. Assume enthalpy and entropy changes of reactions do not depend on temperature.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{CO2(g)} & \ce{CO(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} & \ce{Zn(s)} & \ce{Zn(l)} & \ce{Zn(g)} & \ce{ZnO(s)} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ_{298}\ /\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & -393.5 & -110.5 & & & 6.5 & 130.4 & -350.5 \\ \hline S^\circ_{298}\ /\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & 213.8 & 197.7 & 205.1 & 41.7 & 50.8 & 161.0 & 43.7 \\ \hline \text{Melting Point / K} & & & & 692.7 & & & 2247 \\ \hline \text{Boiling Point / K} & & & & & 1180 & & \end{array}$$

Photochemical reduction of carbon dioxide is a promising approach both for solar energy conversion and for reduction of $\ce{CO2}$ content in the atmosphere. There are several ways to convert $\ce{CO2}$ to CO and other useful substances.

Direct decomposition

Direct decomposition of $\ce{CO2}$ to CO and $\ce{O2}$ is a highly endothermic process which requires a large amount of energy – from heat or from light.

6.1 Estimate the temperature (in K) at which half of $\ce{CO2}$ decomposes at equilibrium at a total pressure of 1 bar.

Catalytic decomposition

The use of metal/metal oxide catalytic systems allows the temperature of $\ce{CO2}$ decomposition to be significantly reduced and eases the separation of the gaseous products by using thermochemical cycles.

Consider a catalytic cycle based on the Zn/ZnO system and containing two reactions. The net reaction is $\ce{CO2}$ decomposition into CO and $\ce{O2}$. Reaction 1 is exothermic, while Reaction 2 is highly endothermic – the reactants should be heated to the required temperature.

6.2 Write equations for Reaction 1 and Reaction 2.

The operating temperature for Reaction 1 is $1073\,\mathrm{K}$.

6.3 Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K$, for Reaction 1 and find the degree of $\ce{CO2}$ conversion, $x$, at this temperature.

Reaction 2 is performed at the much higher temperature of $2000\,\mathrm{K}$.

6.4 Calculate the equilibrium pressure of oxygen, $p(\ce{O2})$, in bar, at this temperature.

Photocatalytic reduction

Photocatalytic reduction of $\ce{CO2}$ with water is akin to natural photosynthesis. Plants convert $\ce{CO2}$ to carbohydrates as an energy source, but human civilisation needs hydrocarbons to produce energy. On the way from $\ce{CO2}$ to $\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y$ there are many possible intermediate products of $\ce{CO2}$ reduction.

Visible light ($400\,\mathrm{nm} < \lambda < 700\,\mathrm{nm}$) makes up >40% of the total solar radiation reaching Earth. Light can be absorbed by semiconductors or dyes, leading to electronic excitation which can promote redox reactions. The band gaps of some common semiconductors are listed.

In an early photocatalysis experiment, SiC semiconductor was suspended in $V = 100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water, and $\ce{CO2}$ was bubbled through at a rate of $v = 3.0\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}$ ($T = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $p = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$). The suspension was irradiated by a $P = 500\,\mathrm{W}$ lamp ($\lambda = 365\,\mathrm{nm}$) for $t = 7\,\mathrm{h}$. After irradiation, the solution contained $c(\ce{HCHO}) = 1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$ and $c(\ce{CH3OH}) = 5.4\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$.

The apparent quantum yield $\phi$ is defined as:

$$\phi = \frac{N_e}{N_i},$$

where $N_e$ is the number of electrons transferred and $N_i$ is the number of incident photons.

problems.problem:
Problem 1 (7% of the total; 25 points). A journey through time: The secrets of Avicenna

A chemist found herself in the 11th Century, where she met the renowned physician Avicenna. In Avicenna's laboratory, she discovered a blue elixir and a yellow mysterious stone. She brought them back to 2026. Determined to uncover their composition, she began her research.

Part 1. The blue elixir

At first, the chemist compiled a table listing the names of the only four plants which she saw in Avicenna's lab that could have been used to prepare the elixir, and the compounds that can be extracted from these plants.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-1-fig1.png

Using chromatography, she determined that the elixir consists of four different substances ($\textbf{X}$, $\textbf{Y}$, $\textbf{Z}$ and $\textbf{W}$).

The chemist then discovered that $\textbf{X}$ can isomerise into $\textbf{Y}$ in an acidic medium and that $\textbf{Y}$ has a plane of symmetry.

1.1 Identify $\textbf{X}$ and $\textbf{Y}$. (3.0 pt)

Chromatography also revealed it was substance $\textbf{Z}$ that gave the elixir its blue colour. $\textbf{Z}$ is a derivative of the well-known substance $\textbf{A}$, which has two perpendicular planes of symmetry. When heated, $\textbf{A}$ isomerises into aromatic compound $\textbf{B}$, which has three mutually perpendicular planes of symmetry. When substance $\textbf{Z}$ is chlorinated, a pair of peaks with an intensity ratio of 3:1 is observed in the mass spectrum at m/z 218 and 220, respectively.

1.2 Identify $\textbf{Z}$ and draw the structures of substances $\textbf{A}$ and $\textbf{B}$. (4.0 pt)

The chemist extracted $\textbf{W}$ from the elixir. When $\textbf{W}$ was added to an aqueous $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ solution, a characteristic colour change was observed. Mass spectrometric analysis of $\textbf{W}$ revealed the intensity ratio of $[\mathrm{M}]^+ : [\mathrm{M}+1]^+ = 9:1$, where M is the molecular ion. Assume carbon consists exclusively of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{13}\mathrm{C}$, the natural isotopic abundance of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ is 98.9%, and all other elements are monoisotopic.

1.3 Determine the number of carbon atoms ($n$) from the mass spec data and identify $\textbf{W}$. Show your calculations. (3.0 pt)

Part 2. The mysterious stone

Avicenna had told her the $\textbf{stone}$ was a stoichiometric compound. She dissolved it in dilute nitric acid. After that, she adjusted the pH of the solution to ~4 and added NaF. This led to the formation of precipitate $\mathbf{C}\cdot x\ce{H2O}$, which contained 39.16% water by mass. Anhydrous $\textbf{C}$ reacts with an excess of NaF to yield compound $\textbf{D}$, which contains 32.85% sodium and 12.85% of metal $\textbf{Q}$ by mass, and is used in the industrial production of $\textbf{Q}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-1-fig2.png

1.4 Identify metal $\textbf{Q}$ and compounds $\mathbf{C}\cdot x\ce{H2O}$ and $\textbf{D}$. (4.0 pt)

Avicenna told her that he found the $\textbf{stone}$ in a coal deposit. The $\textbf{stone}$ contains the anion of a highly symmetrical acid $\textbf{F}$. Reaction of $\textbf{F}$ with $\ce{P2O5}$ gives binary compound $\textbf{G}$, which contains 49.98% of oxygen by mass and has a three-fold symmetry axis. $\textbf{F}$ can be prepared by oxidising compound $\textbf{E}$ with potassium permanganate in an acidic solution. $\textbf{E}$ contains 11.18% of hydrogen by mass and has a six-fold symmetry axis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-1-fig3.png

1.5 Draw the structures of $\textbf{E}$, $\textbf{F}$, and $\textbf{G}$. (7.0 pt)

Then, she analysed the $\textbf{stone}$ thermogravimetrically in open air. A 10.00 g sample began to lose mass at approximately $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and stopped at 5.75 g at $200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A second drop in mass was observed at $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with a final mass of 1.50 g of compound $\textbf{H}$ remaining constant at higher temperatures.

1.6 Determine the chemical formulae of the $\textbf{stone}$ and compound $\textbf{H}$ using thermogravimetric data. (4.0 pt)

problems.title: Kinetics of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (6% of the total; 35 points). Kinetics of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

When the chemicals $\ce{KBrO3}$, $\ce{CH2(COOH)2}$ (malonic acid, – MA), $\ce{Ce(SO4)2}$, and $\ce{H2SO4}$ are mixed, the concentration, $C$, of Ce species and the colour of the solution oscillates between yellow (due to $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$) and colourless (due to $\ce{Ce^{3+}}$). A schematic picture is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-2-fig1.png

2.1 Write the overall balanced reaction equation of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction (BZ reaction). Note: in this reaction, MA is oxidised to $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{BrO3^-}$ is reduced to $\ce{Br^-}$, and Ce(IV) is a catalyst. (2.0 pt)

The mechanism of the BZ reaction is shown below (BMA – $\ce{CHBr(COOH)2}$):

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} \text{Process A} & (1)\ \ce{HBrO2 + BrO3^- + H+} \xrightarrow{k_1} \ce{2 BrO2^. + H2O} & k_1 = 1.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (2)\ \ce{BrO2^. + Ce^{3+} + H+} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{HBrO2 + Ce^{4+}} & k_2 = 6.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (3)\ \ce{2 HBrO2} \xrightarrow{k_3} \ce{BrO3^- + HBrO + H+} & k_3 = 4.0\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{Process B} & (4)\ \ce{HBrO2 + Br^- + H+} \xrightarrow{k_4} \ce{2 HBrO} & k_4 = 2.0\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (5)\ \ce{BrO3^- + Br^- + 2 H+} \xrightarrow{k_5} \ce{HBrO + HBrO2} & k_5 = 2.1\ \mathrm{M^{-3}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (6)\ \ce{HBrO + MA} \xrightarrow{k_6} \ce{BMA + H2O} & k_6 = 8.2\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{Process C} & (7)\ \ce{Ce^{4+} + BMA} \xrightarrow{k_7} \ce{Ce^{3+} + Br^-} + \text{other products} & k_7 = 1.0\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \end{array}$$

In the BZ reaction, $\textbf{Process C}$ occurs continuously, while $\textbf{Processes A}$ and $\textbf{B}$ alternate with each other. Assume that:

• when $\textbf{Process A}$ occurs the solution is yellow and $\textbf{Process B}$ practically does not occur;
• when $\textbf{Process B}$ occurs the solution is colourless and $\textbf{Process A}$ practically does not occur;
• $[\ce{BrO3^-}]_0 = 0.06$ M, $[\mathrm{MA}]_0 = 0.1$ M, $[\ce{H+}]_0 = 0.8$ M, $[\ce{Ce^{4+}}]_0 = 0.001$ M;
• the concentrations of the reactants (except $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$) and pH are maintained constant throughout the BZ reaction.

2.2 Using the steady-state approximation, calculate the stationary molar concentrations of $\ce{HBrO2}$ in $\textbf{Processes A}$ and $\textbf{B}$, $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{A}$ and $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{B}$. (11.0 pt)

If you could not calculate $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{A}$ and $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{B}$, you can use the values $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{A} = 1\times10^{-5}$ M and $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{B} = 1\times10^{-10}$ M for the following calculations.

During the BZ reaction, the concentrations of $\ce{HBrO2}$ and $\ce{Br^-}$ oscillate strictly in relation to each other, and this is sketched in the phase portrait of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ vs $[\ce{Br^-}]$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-2-fig2.png

Here $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{max}$ is the maximum concentration and $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$ is the critical concentration of $\ce{Br^-}$ at which there is a switch over in processes from $\textbf{A}$ to $\textbf{B}$ or from $\textbf{B}$ to $\textbf{A}$. To switch $\textbf{Process A}$ to $\textbf{Process B}$, the reaction rate of the elementary step (4) must exceed that of the elementary step (1) and vice versa.

2.3 Calculate $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$. (4.0 pt)

If you could not calculate $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$, use $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical} = 1\times10^{-7}$ M for the following calculations.

2.4 In which direction in the phase portrait of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ vs $[\ce{Br^-}]$ will the concentrations of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ and $[\ce{Br^-}]$ change over time? Tick the correct box. (2.0 pt)

The system does not traverse the phase portrait of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ vs $[\ce{Br^-}]$ at a constant velocity, that is the concentration of $[\ce{Br^-}]$ slowly decreases from $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{max} = 7.0\times10^{-4}$ M to $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$, and then almost immediately reaches $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{max}$ again.

2.5 Calculate based on the data the period of oscillations, $\tau$, of the BZ reaction, in seconds. (9.0 pt)

2.6 What will be the effect if the following actions $\textbf{(1-4)}$ are performed on an open system where a BZ reaction is taking place? Tick only one box $\textbf{(a-e)}$ for each case. (4.0 pt)

• 1. Adding of small amount of $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$ during $\textbf{Process A}$.
• 2. Adding of a small amount of $\ce{Ag+}$ during $\textbf{Process B}$.
• 3. Adding of a small amount of $\ce{Br^-}$ during $\textbf{Process B}$.
• 4. Continuous addition of $\ce{Br^-}$.

• [a] prolongs $\textbf{Process A}$
• [b] prolongs $\textbf{Process B}$
• [c] $\textbf{Process A}$ switches to $\textbf{Process B}$
• [d] $\textbf{Process B}$ switches to $\textbf{Process A}$
• [e] oscillations stop

2.7 Which graph qualitatively illustrates the rate of change of Gibbs energy ($\frac{dG}{dt}$) of a $\textbf{closed}$ system in which an oscillatory reaction occurs? Tick the correct box. (3.0 pt)

The main reaction occurring in nuclear power plants is the reaction where $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission, releasing energy and producing three additional neutrons, thus sustaining a chain reaction.

Neutrons that induce the chain reaction are produced by several ways:

• a) Reaction of $^{11}\mathrm{B}$ with $\alpha$-particles inside the reactor core
